3.2 Hard Stochastic attention
This model is a stochastic and sampling-based
process where, at every timestept, we are making
a hard choice to attend only one annotation. This
corresponds to one spatial location in the image.
Hard attention has previously been used in the
context of object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014;
Ba et al., 2015) and later extended to image
description generation (Xu et al., 2015). In the
context of multimodal NMT, we can follow Xu
et al. (2015) because both our models involve the
same process on images.

1 Introduction
In machine translation, neural networks have at-
tracted a lot of research attention. Recently,
the attention-based encoder-decoder framework
(Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2014) has
been largely adopted. In this approach, Recurrent
Neural Networks (RNNs) map source sequences
of words to target sequences. The attention mech-
anism is learned to focus on different parts of the
input sentence while decoding. Attention mecha-
nisms have shown to work with other modalities
too, like images, where their are able to learn to
attend the salient parts of an image, for instance
when generating text captions (Xu et al., 2015).

3.2 Hard Stochastic attention
This model is a stochastic and sampling-based
process where, at every timestept, we are making
a hard choice to attend only one annotation. This
corresponds to one spatial location in the image.
Hard attention has previously been used in the
context of object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014;
Ba et al., 2015) and later extended to image
description generation (Xu et al., 2015). In the
context of multimodal NMT, we can follow Xu
et al. (2015) because both our models involve the
same process on images.

A test set of
size 1000 is used for metrics evaluation. 5.1 Training and model details
All our models are build on top of the nematus
framework (Sennrich et al., 2017). The encoder
is a bidirectional RNN with GRU, one 1024D
single-layer forward and one 1024D single-layer
backward RNN. Word embeddings for source and
target language are of 620D and trained jointly
with the model. Word embeddings and other
non-recurrent matrices are initialized by sampling
from a Gaussian N (0, 0.012), recurrent matrices
are random orthogonal and bias vectors are all
initialized to zero. To create the image annotations used by our
decoder, we used a ResNet-50 pre-trained on
ImageNet and extracted the features of size
14 × 14 × 1024 at its res4f layer (He et al.,
2016). In our experiments, our decoder operates
on the ﬂattened 196 × 1024 (i.e L × D). We
also apply dropout with a probability of 0.5
on the embeddings, on the hidden states in the
bidirectional RNN in the encoder as well as in the
decoder. In the decoder, we also apply dropout
on the text annotations hi, the image features
ai, on both modality context vector and on all
components of the deep output layer before the
readout operation. We apply dropout using one
same mask in all time steps (Gal and Ghahramani,
2016). We also normalize and tokenize English and
German descriptions using the Moses tokenizer
scripts (Koehn et al., 2007). We use the byte pair
encoding algorithm on the train set to convert
space-separated tokens into subwords (Sennrich
et al., 2016), reducing our vocabulary size to
9226 and 14957 words for English and German
respectively. All variants of our attention model were trained
with ADADELTA (Zeiler, 2012), with mini-
batches of size 80 for our monomodal (text-only)
NMT model and 40 for our multimodal NMT. We
apply early stopping for model selection based
on BLEU4 : training is halted if no improvement
on the development set is observed for more than
20 epochs. We use the metrics BLEU4 (Papineni

next section. 5.3 Qualitative results
For space-saving and ergonomic reasons, we
only discuss about the hard stochastic and soft
attention, the latter being a generalization of the
local attention. As we can see in Figure 7, the soft attention model
is looking roughly at the same region of the image
for every decoding step t. Because the words
”hund”(dog), ”wald”(forest) or ”weg”(way) in left
image are objects, they beneﬁt from a high gating
scalar. As a matter of fact, the attention mech-
anism has learned to detect the objects within a
scene (at every time-step, whichever word we
are decoding as shown in the right image) and
the gating scalar has learned to decide whether
or not we have to look at the picture (or more
accurately whether or not we are translating an
object). Without this scalar, the translation scores
undergo a massive drop (as seen in Caglayan
et al. (2016)) which means that the attention
mechanisms don’t really understand the more
complex relationships between objects, what is
really happening in the scene.

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-
tiﬁed some ﬂaws of the current attention mecha-
nisms, we can conclude pretty safely that images
are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

This model is a stochastic and sampling-based
process where, at every timestept, we are making
a hard choice to attend only one annotation. This
corresponds to one spatial location in the image. Hard attention has previously been used in the
context of object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014;
Ba et al., 2015) and later extended to image
description generation (Xu et al., 2015). In the
context of multimodal NMT, we can follow Xu
et al.

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-
tiﬁed some ﬂaws of the current attention mecha-
nisms, we can conclude pretty safely that images
are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

All our models are build on top of the nematus
framework (Sennrich et al., 2017). The encoder
is a bidirectional RNN with GRU, one 1024D
single-layer forward and one 1024D single-layer
backward RNN. Word embeddings for source and
target language are of 620D and trained jointly
with the model. Word embeddings and other
non-recurrent matrices are initialized by sampling
from a Gaussian N (0, 0.012), recurrent matrices
are random orthogonal and bias vectors are all
initialized to zero. To create the image annotations used by our
decoder, we used a ResNet-50 pre-trained on
ImageNet and extracted the features of size

also apply dropout with a probability of 0.5
on the embeddings, on the hidden states in the
bidirectional RNN in the encoder as well as in the
decoder. In the decoder, we also apply dropout
on the text annotations hi, the image features
ai, on both modality context vector and on all
components of the deep output layer before the
readout operation. We apply dropout using one
same mask in all time steps (Gal and Ghahramani,
2016). We also normalize and tokenize English and

scripts (Koehn et al., 2007). We use the byte pair
encoding algorithm on the train set to convert

Recently,
the attention-based encoder-decoder framework
(Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2014) has
been largely adopted. In this approach, Recurrent
Neural Networks (RNNs) map source sequences
of words to target sequences. The attention mech-
anism is learned to focus on different parts of the
input sentence while decoding. Attention mecha-
nisms have shown to work with other modalities
too, like images, where their are able to learn to
attend the salient parts of an image, for instance
when generating text captions (Xu et al., 2015). For such applications, Convolutional Neural Net-
works (CNNs) such as Deep Residual (He et al.,
2016) have shown to work best to represent im-
ages. Multimodal models of texts and images em-
power new applications such as visual question an-
swering or multimodal caption translation. Also,
the grounding of multiple modalities against each
other may enable the model to have a better under-
standing of each modality individually, such as in
natural language understanding applications. In the ﬁeld of Machine Translation (MT), the ef-
ﬁcient integration of multimodal information still
remains a challenging task. It requires combining
diverse modality vector representations with each
other. These vector representations, also called
context vectors, are computed in order the capture
the most relevant information in a modality to out-
put the best translation of a sentence. To investigate the effectiveness of informa-

results of NMT model were those of Huang et al. (2016) who used LSTM fed with global visual

An empirical study on the effectiveness of images in Multimodal Neural
Machine Translation
Jean-Benoit Delbrouck and St´ephane Dupont
TCTS Lab, University of Mons, Belgium
{jean-benoit.delbrouck, stephane.dupont}@umons.ac.be
Abstract
In state-of-the-art Neural Machine Trans-
lation (NMT), an attention mechanism is
used during decoding to enhance the trans-
lation. At every step, the decoder uses this
mechanism to focus on different parts of
the source sentence to gather the most use-
ful information before outputting its tar-
get word. Recently, the effectiveness of
the attention mechanism has also been ex-
plored for multimodal tasks, where it be-
comes possible to focus both on sentence
parts and image regions that they describe. In this paper, we compare several atten-
tion mechanism on the multimodal trans-
lation task (English, image → German)
and evaluate the ability of the model to
make use of images to improve translation. We surpass state-of-the-art scores on the
Multi30k data set, we nevertheless iden-
tify and report different misbehavior of the
machine while translating. 1 Introduction
In machine translation, neural networks have at-
tracted a lot of research attention.

tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-

ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual

input sentence while decoding. Attention mecha-

lation (NMT), an attention mechanism is
used during decoding to enhance the trans-

mechanism to focus on different parts of
the source sentence to gather the most use-
ful information before outputting its tar-

the attention mechanism has also been ex-
plored for multimodal tasks, where it be-
comes possible to focus both on sentence
parts and image regions that they describe.
In this paper, we compare several atten-
tion mechanism on the multimodal trans-
lation task (English, image → German)
and evaluate the ability of the model to
make use of images to improve translation.

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-
tiﬁed some ﬂaws of the current attention mecha-
nisms, we can conclude pretty safely that images
are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

mechanism to focus on different parts of

comes possible to focus both on sentence
parts and image regions that they describe.
In this paper, we compare several atten-
tion mechanism on the multimodal trans-
lation task (English, image → German)
and evaluate the ability of the model to
make use of images to improve translation.

2 Neural Machine Translation
In this section, we detail the neural machine trans-
lation architecture by Bahdanau et al. (2014), im-
plemented as an attention-based encoder-decoder
framework with recurrent neural networks ( §2.1). We follow by explaining the conditional GRU
layer (§2.2) - the gating mechanism we chose for
our RNN - and how the model can be ported to a
multimodal version (§2.3). 2.1 Text-based NMT
Given a source sentence X = (x1,x 2,...,x M),
the neural network directly models the condi-
tional probability p(Y |X) of its translation Y =
(y1,y 2,...,y N). The network consists of one en-
coder and one decoder with one attention mecha-
nism. The encoder computes a representation C
for each source sentence and a decoder generates
one target word at a time and by decomposing the
following conditional probability :

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-
tiﬁed some ﬂaws of the current attention mecha-
nisms, we can conclude pretty safely that images
are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

mechanism to focus on different parts of

the attention mechanism has also been ex-
plored for multimodal tasks, where it be-

parts and image regions that they describe.

tion mechanism on the multimodal trans-
lation task (English, image → German)
and evaluate the ability of the model to
make use of images to improve translation.

A test set of
size 1000 is used for metrics evaluation. 5.1 Training and model details
All our models are build on top of the nematus
framework (Sennrich et al., 2017). The encoder
is a bidirectional RNN with GRU, one 1024D
single-layer forward and one 1024D single-layer
backward RNN. Word embeddings for source and
target language are of 620D and trained jointly
with the model. Word embeddings and other
non-recurrent matrices are initialized by sampling
from a Gaussian N (0, 0.012), recurrent matrices
are random orthogonal and bias vectors are all
initialized to zero. To create the image annotations used by our
decoder, we used a ResNet-50 pre-trained on
ImageNet and extracted the features of size
14 × 14 × 1024 at its res4f layer (He et al.,
2016). In our experiments, our decoder operates
on the ﬂattened 196 × 1024 (i.e L × D). We
also apply dropout with a probability of 0.5
on the embeddings, on the hidden states in the
bidirectional RNN in the encoder as well as in the
decoder. In the decoder, we also apply dropout
on the text annotations hi, the image features
ai, on both modality context vector and on all
components of the deep output layer before the
readout operation. We apply dropout using one
same mask in all time steps (Gal and Ghahramani,
2016). We also normalize and tokenize English and
German descriptions using the Moses tokenizer
scripts (Koehn et al., 2007). We use the byte pair
encoding algorithm on the train set to convert
space-separated tokens into subwords (Sennrich
et al., 2016), reducing our vocabulary size to
9226 and 14957 words for English and German
respectively. All variants of our attention model were trained
with ADADELTA (Zeiler, 2012), with mini-
batches of size 80 for our monomodal (text-only)
NMT model and 40 for our multimodal NMT. We
apply early stopping for model selection based
on BLEU4 : training is halted if no improvement
on the development set is observed for more than
20 epochs. We use the metrics BLEU4 (Papineni
et al., 2002), METEOR (Denkowski and Lavie,
2014) and TER (Snover et al., 2006) to evaluate
the quality of our models’ translations. 5.2 Quantitative results
We notice a nice overall progress over Calixto
et al. (2017) multimodal baseline, especially
when using the stochastic attention. With im-
provements of +1.51 BLEU and -2.2 TER on both
precision-oriented metrics, the model shows a
strong similarity of the n-grams of our candidate
translations with respect to the references. The
more recall-oriented metrics METEOR scores

results.question: How do the soft, hard stochastic, and local attention mechanisms differ in how they attend to the image?
results.answer: The soft attention mechanism attends to the whole image, which can be difficult to learn due to the large number of annotations, while the hard stochastic attention mechanism is modeled as a decision process based on previous choices, allowing for a more focused recall. The local attention mechanism, on the other hand, selects a specific image patch and focuses on a small window of context around it, using the same "zoom" for all target positions. This approach is a trade-off between soft and hard attention, allowing for selective focus while still being differentiable, unlike the stochastic attention which requires more complex training techniques.

results.question: How do the soft, hard stochastic, and local attention mechanisms differ in how they attend to the image?
results.answer: The soft attention mechanism attends to the entire image, generating a context vector as a weighted sum over all annotations, which can be challenging to learn due to the large number of annotations. The hard stochastic attention mechanism, on the other hand, makes a hard choice to attend to only one specific annotation at each time step, corresponding to one spatial location in the image. Local attention selects a small window of context around a specific annotation, using the same "zoom" for all target positions, which allows it to focus on a patch of the image while still being differentiable. Thus, soft attention looks broadly at the image, hard stochastic attention focuses narrowly on one point, and local attention balances between the two by focusing on a small region around a selected annotation.

results.question: What three optimizations do the authors add to the image attention mechanism?
results.answer:
The authors add three optimizations to the image attention mechanism: 

1. A gating scalar βt is computed at every decoding step t based on the previous decoder state, which is used to compute a time-dependent image context vector.
2. The output size of trainable parameters Ua, Wa, and vT is doubled when computing the expected annotations over the image annotation sequence.
3. A Gaussian distribution centered around the aligned position in the annotation sequence is placed on the alphas to favor annotations near that position.

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-

are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

results.question: What three optimizations do the authors add to the image attention mechanism?
results.answer:
The authors add three optimizations to the image attention mechanism: 

1. A gating scalar βt computed at every decoding step t, which emphasizes certain objects in the image descriptions.
2. Doubling the output size of trainable parameters Ua, Wa, and vT when computing expected annotations over the image annotation sequence.
3. The use of a grounding attention mechanism that merges each spatial location in the annotation sequence with the initial decoder state, allowing for the removal of unnecessary information in the image annotations according to the source sentence.

We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the

results.question: What evidence indicates the stochastic-attention model largely ignores the image, and how do the authors explain it?
results.answer:
The evidence indicating that the stochastic-attention model largely ignores the image is found in the description of the hard stochastic attention mechanism, which states that it "is a stochastic and sampling-based process where, at every timestep, we are making a hard choice to attend only one annotation." This implies that the model focuses on a single spatial location in the image rather than considering the entire image context. 

The authors explain this by noting that hard attention has previously been used in object recognition and image description generation, suggesting that it operates by making discrete choices rather than integrating information from multiple locations in the image. This selective attention can lead to a limited understanding of the overall image context, as it does not leverage the full range of spatial information available.

results.question: What evidence indicates the stochastic-attention model largely ignores the image, and how do the authors explain it?
results.answer: The evidence indicating that the stochastic-attention model largely ignores the image is that "a significant amount of sentences don’t have a summed gating scalar ≥ 0.10," which leads to the model totally discarding the image in the translation process. The authors explain this by noting that the gating scalar happens to be really low in the stochastic attention mechanism, suggesting that the model misses important information for a multimodal translation task. They also mention that if the attention loses track of the objects in the picture, the model still takes the image into account but overrides the information brought by the text-based annotations, resulting in misleading translations.

results.question: How does the conditional GRU (cGRU) in the decoder combine its recurrent cells with attention?
results.answer: The conditional GRU (cGRU) in the decoder combines its recurrent cells with attention by using two stacked GRU activations (REC1 and REC2) and an attention mechanism (fatt). At each time-step, REC1 computes a hidden state proposal based on the previous hidden state and the previously emitted word. Then, the attention mechanism computes a context vector (ct) over the source sentence using the annotations sequence and the intermediate hidden state proposal. Finally, REC2 computes the hidden state of the cGRU by looking at the intermediate representation and the context vector. This process allows the cGRU to effectively integrate information from both the previous states and the attention context.

results.question: How does the conditional GRU (cGRU) in the decoder combine its recurrent cells with attention?
results.answer: The conditional GRU (cGRU) combines its recurrent cells with attention through a two-stacked GRU architecture. At each time-step, the first recurrent cell (REC1) computes a hidden state proposal based on the previous hidden state and the previously emitted word. Then, the attention mechanism computes a context vector over the source sentence using the annotations sequence and the intermediate hidden state proposal. Finally, the second recurrent cell (REC2) computes the hidden state of the cGRU by considering the intermediate representation from REC1 and the context vector from the attention mechanism. This process allows the cGRU to effectively integrate attention into its decoding process.

results.question: How does the conditional GRU (cGRU) in the decoder combine its recurrent cells with attention?
results.answer: The conditional GRU (cGRU) in the decoder combines its recurrent cells with attention by using two stacked GRU activations (REC1 and REC2) and an attention mechanism. At each time-step t, REC1 computes a hidden state proposal based on the previous hidden state and the previously emitted word. The attention mechanism then computes a context vector over the source sentence using the annotations and the intermediate hidden state proposal. Finally, REC2 updates the hidden state by incorporating both the previous hidden state and the hidden state proposal, along with the context vector.

size 1000 is used for metrics evaluation. 5.1 Training and model details
All our models are build on top of the nematus
framework (Sennrich et al., 2017). The encoder
is a bidirectional RNN with GRU, one 1024D
single-layer forward and one 1024D single-layer
backward RNN. Word embeddings for source and
target language are of 620D and trained jointly
with the model. Word embeddings and other
non-recurrent matrices are initialized by sampling
from a Gaussian N (0, 0.012), recurrent matrices
are random orthogonal and bias vectors are all
initialized to zero. To create the image annotations used by our
decoder, we used a ResNet-50 pre-trained on
ImageNet and extracted the features of size
14 × 14 × 1024 at its res4f layer (He et al.,
2016). In our experiments, our decoder operates
on the ﬂattened 196 × 1024 (i.e L × D). We
also apply dropout with a probability of 0.5
on the embeddings, on the hidden states in the
bidirectional RNN in the encoder as well as in the
decoder. In the decoder, we also apply dropout
on the text annotations hi, the image features
ai, on both modality context vector and on all
components of the deep output layer before the
readout operation. We apply dropout using one
same mask in all time steps (Gal and Ghahramani,
2016). We also normalize and tokenize English and
German descriptions using the Moses tokenizer
scripts (Koehn et al., 2007). We use the byte pair
encoding algorithm on the train set to convert
space-separated tokens into subwords (Sennrich
et al., 2016), reducing our vocabulary size to
9226 and 14957 words for English and German
respectively. All variants of our attention model were trained
with ADADELTA (Zeiler, 2012), with mini-
batches of size 80 for our monomodal (text-only)
NMT model and 40 for our multimodal NMT. We
apply early stopping for model selection based
on BLEU4 : training is halted if no improvement
on the development set is observed for more than
20 epochs. We use the metrics BLEU4 (Papineni
et al., 2002), METEOR (Denkowski and Lavie,
2014) and TER (Snover et al., 2006) to evaluate
the quality of our models’ translations. 5.2 Quantitative results

6 Conclusion and future work
We have tried different attention mechanism and
tweaks for the image modality. We showed im-
provements and encouraging results overall on the
Flickr30K Entities dataset. Even though we iden-
tiﬁed some ﬂaws of the current attention mecha-
nisms, we can conclude pretty safely that images
are an helpful resource for the machine in a trans-
lation task. We are looking forward to try out
richer and more suitable features for multimodal
translation (ie. dense captioning features). An-
other interesting approach would be to use visu-
ally grounded word embeddings to capture visual
notions of semantic relatedness.

1 Introduction
In machine translation, neural networks have at-
tracted a lot of research attention. Recently,
the attention-based encoder-decoder framework
(Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2014) has
been largely adopted. In this approach, Recurrent
Neural Networks (RNNs) map source sequences
of words to target sequences. The attention mech-
anism is learned to focus on different parts of the
input sentence while decoding. Attention mecha-
nisms have shown to work with other modalities
too, like images, where their are able to learn to
attend the salient parts of an image, for instance
when generating text captions (Xu et al., 2015).

Translation, we used the Multi30K dataset (Elliott
et al., 2016) which is an extended version of the
Flickr30K Entities. For each image, one of the
English descriptions was selected and manually
translated into German by a professional transla-
tor. As training and development data, 29,000 and
1,014 triples are used respectively. A test set of
size 1000 is used for metrics evaluation.
